title: Summarii Temporum
author: Samuel Aniensis
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0249c.stoa001.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: sive sacri sive profani, illa potius tempora inquirerent, divinat quoque Scripturae nos docent, quandoquidem vel ipsis familiaribus suis aiebat ille Vivificus , « Non est vestrum nosse horas et (1) tempora quae Pater posuit in sua potestate1.» Quod effatum non de supremo solum exterminio, sed de temporibus omnibus idcirco pronuntiatum verax ille Eusebius ait (2), ut si qui sunt curiosiores atque inania scrutantes, ii paucis his verbis deterrerentur, quominus doctrinam temporum se assequi posse certa scientia confiderent. Profecto divinum hoc Dominicumque oraculum eo præcipue nomine editum est, ut vanarum rerum exploratores incasso labore supersedeant.
passages.english: whether sacred or profane, should rather investigate those times, the divine Scriptures also teach us, since that Life-giver said even to his own intimates, "It is not for you to know the hours and times which the Father has placed in his own power." That truthful man Eusebius says that this saying was pronounced not about the final destruction alone but about all times, so that if any are rather curious and searching into empty things, they might be deterred by these few words from trusting that they could attain the doctrine of times with certain knowledge. Indeed this divine oracle of the Lord was given forth chiefly on this account, that the explorers of vain matters should desist from fruitless labour.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence (context: "Jam fore ut homines..."); the main verb governing the opening clause is not clear, and "divinat quoque Scripturae nos docent" seems corrupt, read as "divinae quoque Scripturae nos docent". "Vivificus" (Life-giver) renders a Greek epithet of Christ. "incasso" read as "incasso/in cassum" (in vain). Footnote marks (1), (2), 1 omitted.

passages.original: Porro hujus rei testibus utuntur celeberrimis doctissimisque viris, Origene scilicet Gregorioque Theologo atque Epiphanio Cyprio : imo adeo Luca evangelista sancti Spiritus pleno, qui illum in suam genealogiam intulit (24). De horum ergo sententia Abrahamus quidem vicesimum primum locum post Adamum occupat. Summa autem annorum, quos Eusebius ab Adamo ad Abrahamum MMMCLXXXIV scribit, ad MMMCCCIV consurgit.
passages.english: Moreover, they use as witnesses of this matter most celebrated and most learned men, namely Origen and Gregory the Theologian and Epiphanius of Cyprus; indeed even Luke the evangelist, full of the Holy Spirit, who included him in his genealogy. According to their opinion, then, Abraham occupies the twenty-first place after Adam. And the sum of the years from Adam to Abraham, which Eusebius writes as 3184, rises to 3304.
passages.notes: "him" is Cainan, mentioned in the preceding context. Footnote mark (24) omitted.

passages.original: Candaulis hujus historiam narrat Herodotus(80), nempe quod is nimio erga suam conjugem studio elatus, hanc feminarum omnium pulcherrimam existimaverit, nudatamque veslibus Gygi clam demonstraverit ; qua ignominia sapiens uxor ad iracundiam commota occidendum curaverit, sibique virum adsciverit Gygem.
passages.english: Herodotus narrates the story of this Candaules: namely that he, carried away by excessive devotion to his wife, thought her the most beautiful of all women and secretly showed her, stripped of her clothes, to Gyges; and that his wise wife, moved to anger by this disgrace, had him killed and took Gyges as her husband.

passages.original: VII. Artaxcs Longimanus annis XL. Nonnulli Estherem sub hoc exstitisse aiunt: quod ego tamen, inquit Eusebius (83), non probo, quandoquidem Esdræ libri per eam aetatem scripti nullam ejus rei mentionem faciunt.
passages.english: VII. Artaxerxes Longimanus, 40 years. Some say that Esther lived under him; but I, says Eusebius, do not approve this, since the books of Ezra, written in that period, make no mention of this matter.

passages.original: Phlegen etiam, qui olympiades jam inde ab earum primordiis persecutus est, tertio decimo libro diserte ita scribit : « Quarto nimirum anuo ducentesimae tertiae olympiadis magnum solis fuisse defectum, qualem nemo ante animadverterat : septimaque diei hora tantam noctem ingruisse, ut sidera cœlo micarent : ingenti terræ motu Bithyniam agitatam, majoremque Nicææ partem dejectam. » Haec tradit laudatus vir. Atque hoc sane magnum indicium est ejus anni quo Vivificus nester cruciatas est, quia nimirum et Joannes testimonio suo in Evangelio confirmat. (50), post quintam decimum Tibcrii annum trietericam prædicationem Christi fuisse. Haud procul eo tempore narrat etiam Josephus, per dies Pentecostes stridorem quemdam motumque primo circa ,sacerdotes esse excitatuiu, mox subitam vocem e penetratibus templi in haec verba erupisse: « Digrediamur hinc, digrediamur. » Idem insuper scribit Josephus, Pilatum pfaesidem sub id tempus noctu imaginem Cesaris in templo contra vetitum collocandam curasse : quae res magni tumultus scditionisque Judaeorum causa fuit.
passages.english: Phlegon also, who traced the Olympiads from their very beginnings, writes explicitly in his thirteenth book as follows: "In the fourth year of the two hundred and third Olympiad there was a great eclipse of the sun, such as no one had noticed before; and at the seventh hour of the day so great a night came on that the stars shone in the sky; Bithynia was shaken by a huge earthquake, and the greater part of Nicaea was thrown down." This is what the man cited reports. And this is indeed a great indication of the year in which our Life-giver was crucified, since John too confirms by his testimony in the Gospel that the preaching of Christ lasted three years after the fifteenth year of Tiberius. Josephus also relates that not far from that time, during the days of Pentecost, a certain rustling and movement was first stirred up around the priests, and soon a sudden voice burst from the inner sanctuary of the temple in these words: "Let us depart from here, let us depart." The same Josephus writes moreover that about that time Pilate the governor had an image of Caesar set up in the temple by night, contrary to prohibition; this affair was the cause of a great tumult and sedition of the Jews.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (Phlegen = Phlegon, anuo, nester, cruciatas, Tibcrii, excitatuiu, penetratibus = penetralibus, pfaesidem, scditionis). "trietericam" taken as three-year. Footnote mark (50) omitted.

passages.original: Tandem supremo templi exterminio Tilus Judaeos obsedit, Hierosolyma a fundamentis evertit, atque hominum sex myriades caede corrupit. Imo, ut tradit Josephus, fame et gladio centum ac viginti myriades consamptae sunt, abductae autem in captivitatem quadraginta et duodecim myriades.
passages.english: At last, at the final destruction of the temple, Titus besieged the Jews, overthrew Jerusalem from its foundations, and slaughtered sixty thousand people. Indeed, as Josephus reports, one million two hundred thousand were consumed by famine and sword, and four hundred and twenty thousand were led away into captivity.
passages.notes: "Tilus" read as "Titus". "quadraginta et duodecim myriades" literally "forty and twelve myriads" (520,000?); the phrase is odd and may be corrupt; Josephus' figure for captives is 97,000. Translated as 420,000 is uncertain; literally it gives 520,000.
